weak_points: All decision variables are declared as continuous; production units are physically discrete, so integer (or at least non-negative integer) types would be more appropriate for x_{i,t}, I_{i,t}, and L_{i,t}.

No explicit mutual-exclusion constraint prevents I_{i,t} and L_{i,t} from being simultaneously positive in the same period; although the objective naturally discourages this, a constraint such as I_{i,t} * L_{i,t} = 0 (or a big-M linearization) would make the model logically tighter.

The end-of-horizon inventory requirement is modeled as I_{i,4} >= 150 (at least 150). The problem states 'required to have 150 units in stock,' which could be read as an exact target; if the intent is exactly 150, an equality constraint would be needed.

No explicit upper bounds are placed on individual production variables x_{i,t}; while the quarterly capacity constraints implicitly bound them, adding per-product upper bounds (e.g., derived from capacity / hours-per-unit) would improve numerical conditioning and solver performance.

The balance equations use the net-position form (I_{i,t} - L_{i,t} = I_{i,t-1} - L_{i,t-1} + x_{i,t} - D_{i,t}), which is valid but couples inventory and backorder into a single scalar; a formulation with separate inventory and backorder balance equations (I_{i,t} = I_{i,t-1} + x_{i,t} - D_{i,t} + L_{i,t-1} - L_{i,t}) would make the physical interpretation more transparent and avoid potential solver confusion with the sign of the net position.

weak_points: Complementarity constraints (I_{i,t} * L_{i,t} = 0) are bilinear and make the problem a MINLP, yet they are fully redundant: the balance equation I_{i,t} - L_{i,t} = (net position) combined with I_{i,t} >= 0 and L_{i,t} >= 0 already forces at most one of I or L to be positive in any feasible solution. Removing them yields an equivalent MILP that is far easier to solve.

The separate inventory (I) and backorder (L) variable design is the root cause of the non-linearity. A cleaner formulation would use a single signed net-position variable (e.g., S_{i,t} = I_{i,t} - L_{i,t}) that can be negative, then define the cost terms as 5*max(0,S) + penalty*max(0,-S) via auxiliary linear constraints, keeping the model fully linear.

The upper bound on x_1_2 is listed as 7500 even though the no-production constraint x_1_2 = 0 is imposed separately; while not incorrect, setting the bound to [0,0] directly would tighten the formulation and avoid a redundant constraint.

The end-of-horizon requirement is modeled as I_{i,4} >= 150 (inequality). The problem states 'required to have 150 units in stock,' which is naturally a minimum, so this is acceptable, but the formulation does not explicitly state that all outstanding backorders must be cleared by Q4 (L_{i,4} = 0). This is implicitly enforced by the balance equation when I_{i,4} >= 150 > 0, but making it explicit would improve clarity and robustness if the complementarity constraints are removed.

[export_rebinding_v1]
When business variables exist under different solver names, bind names instead of rewriting the model. Preserve the objective and constraints. Positive evidence: IDs 4, 8 and 25 passed independent audit after rebinding with unchanged objectives. Counterexample: ID 48 lacks total production roles, so name-only rebinding is insufficient; add missing roles instead.
Source: work/industryor_semantic_dag_dev_v0.2

[indicator_bidirectional_v1]
A binary indicator must be consistent with positive quantity in both directions: indicator <= quantity and quantity <= independent_upper_bound * indicator. Do not invent the upper bound. Positive evidence: IDs 9, 19, 20 and 21 recovered after scoped repair. Counterexample: indicator repair alone cannot fix a wrong business objective.
Source: work/industryor_semantic_dag_dev_v0.2

[objective_consistency_v1]
Recompute the business objective from semantic variables and check its direction. Goal-programming deviations are not business profit. ID 48 had feasible variables and an independent business optimum but a mismatched reported objective, and must remain rejected. Never inject a target value.
Source: work/industryor_semantic_dag_dev_v0.2/prob_048/branch_dag/regenerate/score.json

[regenerate_rebind_v1]
After regeneration, stale aliases can erase the export. Remove aliases whose solver names no longer exist, prefer verified canonical names, and rebind if needed. Rebinding completes evidence but does not prove business correctness. ID 48 demonstrates that objective semantics still need independent verification.
Source: work/industryor_semantic_dag_dev_v0.2/prob_048/branch_dag/regenerate/score.json

[dynamic_collection_binding_v1]
Dictionary comprehensions and simple loops may bind semantic names to expressions such as x['A']. Use only constant, code-verified index sets when repairing them. Do not guess nested or dynamic bindings. ID 19 supports this scoped mechanism; unsupported structures remain UNKNOWN.
Source: work/industryor_semantic_dag_dev_v0.2/prob_019/branch_dag/dag.json

weak_points: Balance equations for quarters 2–4 are missing the '−L_{i,t−1}' term: the correct form should be I_{i,t} − L_{i,t} = I_{i,t−1} − L_{i,t−1} + x_{i,t} − D_{i,t}. As written, the prior-period backlog is dropped, so L_{i,t} captures only the current-period shortfall rather than the cumulative unmet demand.

Because the backlog is not carried forward, the penalty term in the objective (20·ΣL for I/II, 10·ΣL for III) underestimates the true cost: a unit delayed by two quarters is charged only one quarter's penalty instead of two.

A later formulation should either (a) add the −L_{i,t−1} term to every balance equation for t≥2, or (b) introduce an explicit cumulative-backlog variable B_{i,t} with its own recurrence B_{i,t} = max(0, B_{i,t−1} + D_{i,t} − I_{i,t−1} − x_{i,t}) and charge the penalty on B_{i,t}.

The end-of-horizon inventory constraint I_{i,4} ≥ 150 is stated as a lower bound; while the optimizer will typically set it to exactly 150, the formulation should clarify whether the requirement is 'at least' or 'exactly' 150 units to avoid ambiguity in edge cases where excess inventory is free.

weak_points: All decision variables are declared as continuous; production units are physically discrete, so integer (or at least non-negative integer) types would be more appropriate for x_{i,t}, I_{i,t}, and L_{i,t}.

No explicit mutual-exclusion constraint prevents I_{i,t} and L_{i,t} from being simultaneously positive in the same period; although the objective naturally discourages this, a constraint such as I_{i,t} * L_{i,t} = 0 (or a big-M linearization) would make the model logically tighter.

The end-of-horizon inventory requirement is modeled as I_{i,4} >= 150 (at least 150). The problem states 'required to have 150 units in stock,' which could be read as an exact target; if the intent is exactly 150, an equality constraint would be needed.

No explicit upper bounds are placed on individual production variables x_{i,t}; while the quarterly capacity constraints implicitly bound them, adding per-product upper bounds (e.g., derived from capacity / hours-per-unit) would improve numerical conditioning and solver performance.

The balance equations use the net-position form (I_{i,t} - L_{i,t} = I_{i,t-1} - L_{i,t-1} + x_{i,t} - D_{i,t}), which is valid but couples inventory and backorder into a single scalar; a formulation with separate inventory and backorder balance equations (I_{i,t} = I_{i,t-1} + x_{i,t} - D_{i,t} + L_{i,t-1} - L_{i,t}) would make the physical interpretation more transparent and avoid potential solver confusion with the sign of the net position.

weak_points: Complementarity constraints (I_{i,t} * L_{i,t} = 0) are bilinear and make the problem a MINLP, yet they are fully redundant: the balance equation I_{i,t} - L_{i,t} = (net position) combined with I_{i,t} >= 0 and L_{i,t} >= 0 already forces at most one of I or L to be positive in any feasible solution. Removing them yields an equivalent MILP that is far easier to solve.

The separate inventory (I) and backorder (L) variable design is the root cause of the non-linearity. A cleaner formulation would use a single signed net-position variable (e.g., S_{i,t} = I_{i,t} - L_{i,t}) that can be negative, then define the cost terms as 5*max(0,S) + penalty*max(0,-S) via auxiliary linear constraints, keeping the model fully linear.

The upper bound on x_1_2 is listed as 7500 even though the no-production constraint x_1_2 = 0 is imposed separately; while not incorrect, setting the bound to [0,0] directly would tighten the formulation and avoid a redundant constraint.

The end-of-horizon requirement is modeled as I_{i,4} >= 150 (inequality). The problem states 'required to have 150 units in stock,' which is naturally a minimum, so this is acceptable, but the formulation does not explicitly state that all outstanding backorders must be cleared by Q4 (L_{i,4} = 0). This is implicitly enforced by the balance equation when I_{i,4} >= 150 > 0, but making it explicit would improve clarity and robustness if the complementarity constraints are removed.

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

warehouses = ["Verona", "Perugia", "Rome", "Pescara", "Taranto", "Lamezia"]
ports = ["Genoa", "Venice", "Ancona", "Naples", "Bari"]

supply = {

    "Rome": 20,

}

demand = {

}

    ("Pescara", "Genoa"): 655,

    ("Pescara", "Ancona"): 155,
    ("Pescara", "Naples"): 240,

    ("Lamezia", "Venice"): 1097,
    ("Lamezia", "Ancona"): 747,
    ("Lamezia", "Naples"): 372,
    ("Lamezia", "Bari"): 333
}

cost_per_km = 30

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

x = {}
for i in warehouses:
    for j in ports:
        x[i, j] = m.addVar(vtype="I", lb=0, ub=supply[i], name=f"x_{i}_{j}")

# Objective: minimize total cost

m.setObjective(quicksum(obj_terms), "minimize")

# Supply constraints

    m.addCons(quicksum(x[i, j] for j in ports) <= supply[i], name=f"supply_{i}")

# Demand constraints
for j in ports:
    m.addCons(quicksum(x[i, j] for i in warehouses) == demand[j], name=f"demand_{j}")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")

weak_points: The truck capacity constraint (each truck carries at most 2 containers) is entirely absent from the formulation. The problem explicitly states this, and it fundamentally changes the cost structure: cost is 30 €/km per truck, not per container, so shipping 2 containers on one truck costs 30·d, not 2·30·d.

No integer variables are introduced to represent the number of trucks dispatched on each (warehouse, port) route. A correct formulation would need variables t_ij ≥ 0 (integer) with the linking constraint x_ij ≤ 2·t_ij.

The objective function uses a purely linear per-container cost (30·d_ij·x_ij), which implicitly assumes each container pays the full truck cost independently. The true cost for route (i,j) should be 30·d_ij·⌈x_ij/2⌉, a piecewise-linear (non-linear) function of the flow, requiring the auxiliary truck variables to linearize.

Because the truck-based cost is non-linear in x_ij, the problem is not a standard linear transportation problem; the candidate formulation silently reduces it to one, potentially yielding a sub-optimal (over-costed) solution whenever a route carries an odd number of containers.

The problem statement asks to 'solve it using COPTPY,' but the formulation provides no implementation skeleton, solver call, or solution-extraction code, leaving the deliverable incomplete relative to the stated requirement.

weak_points: Cost interpretation ambiguity: the problem states 'the cost to transport each container is proportional to the distance traveled by the trucks, with a rate of 30 euros per kilometer.' The formulation interprets this as a per-truck-per-km cost (30*d_ij*t_ij), but the wording 'each container' could equally support a per-container cost (30*d_ij*x_ij), which would make the truck variables and ceiling-link constraints irrelevant to the objective and reduce the problem to a standard transportation model.

Variable upper bounds are inconsistently derived: some x variables are bounded by the warehouse supply (e.g., x_Rome_Genoa ≤ 20), others by the port demand (e.g., x_Rome_Venice ≤ 15), and t variables similarly mix supply-based and demand-based ceilings. While all are valid tightenings, the lack of a uniform rule (e.g., min(supply_i, demand_j)) makes the formulation harder to verify and maintain.

The formulation introduces 30 truck variables (t_ij) and 60 linking constraints (capacity + ceiling) solely to linearize the ceiling function. Because the objective is linear in t and the constraints force t_ij = ceil(x_ij/2) at optimality, an alternative formulation could eliminate t entirely by using a piecewise or big-M approach, or by noting that the cost per container on route (i,j) is 30*d_ij/2 when x_ij is even and 30*d_ij when x_ij is odd—though this would introduce non-linearity. The current approach is valid but adds significant model size.

No explicit non-negativity constraints are listed as separate entries; they are implied by the lower bound of 0 in the variable bounds. While functionally equivalent, a formal mathematical program typically states x_ij ≥ 0 and t_ij ≥ 0 as explicit constraints for clarity and solver compatibility.

weak_points: The truck capacity constraint (each truck carries at most 2 containers) is entirely absent from the formulation. The problem explicitly states this, and it fundamentally changes the cost structure: cost is 30 €/km per truck, not per container, so shipping 2 containers on one truck costs 30·d, not 2·30·d.

No integer variables are introduced to represent the number of trucks dispatched on each (warehouse, port) route. A correct formulation would need variables t_ij ≥ 0 (integer) with the linking constraint x_ij ≤ 2·t_ij.

The objective function uses a purely linear per-container cost (30·d_ij·x_ij), which implicitly assumes each container pays the full truck cost independently. The true cost for route (i,j) should be 30·d_ij·⌈x_ij/2⌉, a piecewise-linear (non-linear) function of the flow, requiring the auxiliary truck variables to linearize.

Because the truck-based cost is non-linear in x_ij, the problem is not a standard linear transportation problem; the candidate formulation silently reduces it to one, potentially yielding a sub-optimal (over-costed) solution whenever a route carries an odd number of containers.

The problem statement asks to 'solve it using COPTPY,' but the formulation provides no implementation skeleton, solver call, or solution-extraction code, leaving the deliverable incomplete relative to the stated requirement.

weak_points: Cost interpretation ambiguity: the problem states 'the cost to transport each container is proportional to the distance traveled by the trucks, with a rate of 30 euros per kilometer,' which could be read as 30 €/km per container (making the objective sum 30*d_ij*x_ij and reducing the problem to a standard transportation model with a capacity side-constraint) rather than 30 €/km per truck as the formulation assumes. A later formulation should explicitly justify or clarify this interpretation.

Variable bounds on x_{i,j} are set to the warehouse supply only; they could be tightened to min(supply_i, demand_j) to reduce the search space (e.g., x_Verona_Genoa ≤ min(10,20)=10 is fine, but x_Lamezia_Bari ≤ min(40,21)=21 would be tighter than 40).

The formulation introduces 60 variables (30 x + 30 t) and 41 constraints; while correct, the t variables and their linking constraints are only needed because of the per-truck cost interpretation. If the cost were per container, the t variables and 30 truck-capacity constraints would be unnecessary, yielding a much simpler LP. The formulation should note this dependency on the cost interpretation.

No explicit lower-bound linking constraint t_{i,j} ≥ ceil(x_{i,j}/2) is stated; correctness relies on the combination of x ≤ 2t, integrality, and the minimization objective to force t to its minimum. While valid, a later formulation could add the complementary constraint t_{i,j} ≥ (x_{i,j}+1)/2 (or equivalently 2*t_{i,j} - x_{i,j} ≤ 1) to make the coupling explicit and aid solver performance.

weak_points: Cost interpretation ambiguity: the problem states 'the cost to transport each container is proportional to the distance traveled by the trucks, with a rate of 30 euros per kilometer.' The formulation interprets this as a per-truck-per-km cost (30*d_ij*t_ij), but the wording 'each container' could equally support a per-container cost (30*d_ij*x_ij), which would make the truck variables and ceiling-link constraints irrelevant to the objective and reduce the problem to a standard transportation model.

Variable upper bounds are inconsistently derived: some x variables are bounded by the warehouse supply (e.g., x_Rome_Genoa ≤ 20), others by the port demand (e.g., x_Rome_Venice ≤ 15), and t variables similarly mix supply-based and demand-based ceilings. While all are valid tightenings, the lack of a uniform rule (e.g., min(supply_i, demand_j)) makes the formulation harder to verify and maintain.

The formulation introduces 30 truck variables (t_ij) and 60 linking constraints (capacity + ceiling) solely to linearize the ceiling function. Because the objective is linear in t and the constraints force t_ij = ceil(x_ij/2) at optimality, an alternative formulation could eliminate t entirely by using a piecewise or big-M approach, or by noting that the cost per container on route (i,j) is 30*d_ij/2 when x_ij is even and 30*d_ij when x_ij is odd—though this would introduce non-linearity. The current approach is valid but adds significant model size.

No explicit non-negativity constraints are listed as separate entries; they are implied by the lower bound of 0 in the variable bounds. While functionally equivalent, a formal mathematical program typically states x_ij ≥ 0 and t_ij ≥ 0 as explicit constraints for clarity and solver compatibility.

weak_points: The truck capacity constraint (each truck carries at most 2 containers) is entirely absent from the formulation. The problem explicitly states this, and it fundamentally changes the cost structure: cost is 30 €/km per truck, not per container, so shipping 2 containers on one truck costs 30·d, not 2·30·d.

No integer variables are introduced to represent the number of trucks dispatched on each (warehouse, port) route. A correct formulation would need variables t_ij ≥ 0 (integer) with the linking constraint x_ij ≤ 2·t_ij.

The objective function uses a purely linear per-container cost (30·d_ij·x_ij), which implicitly assumes each container pays the full truck cost independently. The true cost for route (i,j) should be 30·d_ij·⌈x_ij/2⌉, a piecewise-linear (non-linear) function of the flow, requiring the auxiliary truck variables to linearize.

Because the truck-based cost is non-linear in x_ij, the problem is not a standard linear transportation problem; the candidate formulation silently reduces it to one, potentially yielding a sub-optimal (over-costed) solution whenever a route carries an odd number of containers.

The problem statement asks to 'solve it using COPTPY,' but the formulation provides no implementation skeleton, solver call, or solution-extraction code, leaving the deliverable incomplete relative to the stated requirement.

weak_points: Cost interpretation ambiguity: the problem states 'the cost to transport each container is proportional to the distance traveled by the trucks, with a rate of 30 euros per kilometer,' which could be read as 30 €/km per container (making the objective sum 30*d_ij*x_ij and reducing the problem to a standard transportation model with a capacity side-constraint) rather than 30 €/km per truck as the formulation assumes. A later formulation should explicitly justify or clarify this interpretation.

Variable bounds on x_{i,j} are set to the warehouse supply only; they could be tightened to min(supply_i, demand_j) to reduce the search space (e.g., x_Verona_Genoa ≤ min(10,20)=10 is fine, but x_Lamezia_Bari ≤ min(40,21)=21 would be tighter than 40).

The formulation introduces 60 variables (30 x + 30 t) and 41 constraints; while correct, the t variables and their linking constraints are only needed because of the per-truck cost interpretation. If the cost were per container, the t variables and 30 truck-capacity constraints would be unnecessary, yielding a much simpler LP. The formulation should note this dependency on the cost interpretation.

No explicit lower-bound linking constraint t_{i,j} ≥ ceil(x_{i,j}/2) is stated; correctness relies on the combination of x ≤ 2t, integrality, and the minimization objective to force t to its minimum. While valid, a later formulation could add the complementary constraint t_{i,j} ≥ (x_{i,j}+1)/2 (or equivalently 2*t_{i,j} - x_{i,j} ≤ 1) to make the coupling explicit and aid solver performance.

weak_points: Cost interpretation ambiguity: the problem states 'the cost to transport each container is proportional to the distance traveled by the trucks, with a rate of 30 euros per kilometer.' The formulation interprets this as a per-truck-per-km cost (30*d_ij*t_ij), but the wording 'each container' could equally support a per-container cost (30*d_ij*x_ij), which would make the truck variables and ceiling-link constraints irrelevant to the objective and reduce the problem to a standard transportation model.

Variable upper bounds are inconsistently derived: some x variables are bounded by the warehouse supply (e.g., x_Rome_Genoa ≤ 20), others by the port demand (e.g., x_Rome_Venice ≤ 15), and t variables similarly mix supply-based and demand-based ceilings. While all are valid tightenings, the lack of a uniform rule (e.g., min(supply_i, demand_j)) makes the formulation harder to verify and maintain.

The formulation introduces 30 truck variables (t_ij) and 60 linking constraints (capacity + ceiling) solely to linearize the ceiling function. Because the objective is linear in t and the constraints force t_ij = ceil(x_ij/2) at optimality, an alternative formulation could eliminate t entirely by using a piecewise or big-M approach, or by noting that the cost per container on route (i,j) is 30*d_ij/2 when x_ij is even and 30*d_ij when x_ij is odd—though this would introduce non-linearity. The current approach is valid but adds significant model size.

No explicit non-negativity constraints are listed as separate entries; they are implied by the lower bound of 0 in the variable bounds. While functionally equivalent, a formal mathematical program typically states x_ij ≥ 0 and t_ij ≥ 0 as explicit constraints for clarity and solver compatibility.

[export_rebinding_v1]
When business variables exist under different solver names, bind names instead of rewriting the model. Preserve the objective and constraints. Positive evidence: IDs 4, 8 and 25 passed independent audit after rebinding with unchanged objectives. Counterexample: ID 48 lacks total production roles, so name-only rebinding is insufficient; add missing roles instead.

[indicator_bidirectional_v1]
A binary indicator must be consistent with positive quantity in both directions: indicator <= quantity and quantity <= independent_upper_bound * indicator. Do not invent the upper bound. Positive evidence: IDs 9, 19, 20 and 21 recovered after scoped repair. Counterexample: indicator repair alone cannot fix a wrong business objective.
Source: work/industryor_semantic_dag_dev_v0.2

[objective_consistency_v1]
Recompute the business objective from semantic variables and check its direction. Goal-programming deviations are not business profit. ID 48 had feasible variables and an independent business optimum but a mismatched reported objective, and must remain rejected. Never inject a target value.

[regenerate_rebind_v1]
After regeneration, stale aliases can erase the export. Remove aliases whose solver names no longer exist, prefer verified canonical names, and rebind if needed. Source: work/industryor_semantic_dag_dev_v0.2/prob_048/branch_dag/regenerate/score.json

[dynamic_collection_binding_v1]

weak_points: The truck capacity constraint (each truck carries at most 2 containers) is entirely absent from the formulation. The problem explicitly states this, and it fundamentally changes the cost structure: cost is 30 €/km per truck, not per container, so shipping 2 containers on one truck costs 30·d, not 2·30·d.

No integer variables are introduced to represent the number of trucks dispatched on each (warehouse, port) route. A correct formulation would need variables t_ij ≥ 0 (integer) with the linking constraint x_ij ≤ 2·t_ij.

The objective function uses a purely linear per-container cost (30·d_ij·x_ij), which implicitly assumes each container pays the full truck cost independently. The true cost for route (i,j) should be 30·d_ij·⌈x_ij/2⌉, a piecewise-linear (non-linear) function of the flow, requiring the auxiliary truck variables to linearize.

Because the truck-based cost is non-linear in x_ij, the problem is not a standard linear transportation problem; the candidate formulation silently reduces it to one, potentially yielding a sub-optimal (over-costed) solution whenever a route carries an odd number of containers.

The problem statement asks to 'solve it using COPTPY,' but the formulation provides no implementation skeleton, solver call, or solution-extraction code, leaving the deliverable incomplete relative to the stated requirement.

A later formulation should explicitly justify or clarify this interpretation.

Variable bounds on x_{i,j} are set to the warehouse supply only; they could be tightened to min(supply_i, demand_j) to reduce the search space (e.g., x_Verona_Genoa ≤ min(10,20)=10 is fine, but x_Lamezia_Bari ≤ min(40,21)=21 would be tighter than 40).

The formulation introduces 60 variables (30 x + 30 t) and 41 constraints; while correct, the t variables and their linking constraints are only needed because of the per-truck cost interpretation. If the cost were per container, the t variables and 30 truck-capacity constraints would be unnecessary, yielding a much simpler LP. The formulation should note this dependency on the cost interpretation.

No explicit lower-bound linking constraint t_{i,j} ≥ ceil(x_{i,j}/2) is stated; correctness relies on the combination of x ≤ 2t, integrality, and the minimization objective to force t to its minimum. While valid, a later formulation could add the complementary constraint t_{i,j} ≥ (x_{i,j}+1)/2 (or equivalently 2*t_{i,j} - x_{i,j} ≤ 1) to make the coupling explicit and aid solver performance.

weak_points: Cost interpretation ambiguity: the problem states 'the cost to transport each container is proportional to the distance traveled by the trucks, with a rate of 30 euros per kilometer.' The formulation interprets this as a per-truck-per-km cost (30*d_ij*t_ij), but the wording 'each container' could equally support a per-container cost (30*d_ij*x_ij), which would make the truck variables and ceiling-link constraints irrelevant to the objective and reduce the problem to a standard transportation model.

Variable upper bounds are inconsistently derived: some x variables are bounded by the warehouse supply (e.g., x_Rome_Genoa ≤ 20), others by the port demand (e.g., x_Rome_Venice ≤ 15), and t variables similarly mix supply-based and demand-based ceilings. While all are valid tightenings, the lack of a uniform rule (e.g., min(supply_i, demand_j)) makes the formulation harder to verify and maintain.

The formulation introduces 30 truck variables (t_ij) and 60 linking constraints (capacity + ceiling) solely to linearize the ceiling function. Because the objective is linear in t and the constraints force t_ij = ceil(x_ij/2) at optimality, an alternative formulation could eliminate t entirely by using a piecewise or big-M approach, or by noting that the cost per container on route (i,j) is 30*d_ij/2 when x_ij is even and 30*d_ij when x_ij is odd—though this would introduce non-linearity. The current approach is valid but adds significant model size.

No explicit non-negativity constraints are listed as separate entries; they are implied by the lower bound of 0 in the variable bounds. While functionally equivalent, a formal mathematical program typically states x_ij ≥ 0 and t_ij ≥ 0 as explicit constraints for clarity and solver compatibility.

    ("Lamezia", "Venice"): 1097,
    ("Lamezia", "Ancona"): 747,
    ("Lamezia", "Naples"): 372,
    ("Lamezia", "Bari"): 333
}

cost_per_km = 30

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

x = {}
for i in warehouses:
    for j in ports:
        x[i, j] = m.addVar(vtype="I", lb=0, ub=supply[i], name=f"x_{i}_{j}")

# Objective: minimize total cost
obj_terms = [cost_per_km * dist[i, j] * x[i, j] for i in warehouses for j in ports]
m.setObjective(quicksum(obj_terms), "minimize")

# Supply constraints
for i in warehouses:
    m.addCons(quicksum(x[i, j] for j in ports) <= supply[i], name=f"supply_{i}")

# Demand constraints
for j in ports:
    m.addCons(quicksum(x[i, j] for i in warehouses) == demand[j], name=f"demand_{j}")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

# Data: hours required by each worker for each task
# Workers: 1=I, 2=II, 3=III, 4=IV, 5=V
# Tasks: A, B, C, D
costs = {
    (1, 'A'): 9,  (1, 'B'): 4,  (1, 'C'): 3,  (1, 'D'): 7,
    (2, 'A'): 4,  (2, 'B'): 6,  (2, 'C'): 5,  (2, 'D'): 6,
    (3, 'A'): 5,  (3, 'B'): 4,  (3, 'C'): 7,  (3, 'D'): 5,
    (4, 'A'): 7,  (4, 'B'): 5,  (4, 'C'): 2,  (4, 'D'): 3,
    (5, 'A'): 10, (5, 'B'): 6,  (5, 'C'): 7,  (5, 'D'): 4,
}

workers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
tasks = ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables: binary x_{i,j}
x = {}
for i in workers:
    for j in tasks:
        x[(i, j)] = m.addVar(vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1, name=f"x_{i}_{j}")

# Objective: minimize total working hours
obj = quicksum(costs[(i, j)] * x[(i, j)] for i in workers for j in tasks)
m.setObjective(obj, "minimize")

# Constraints: each task assigned to exactly one worker
for j in tasks:
    m.addCons(quicksum(x[(i, j)] for i in workers) == 1, name=f"task_{j}_assigned")

# Constraints: each worker assigned to at most one task
for i in workers:
    m.addCons(quicksum(x[(i, j)] for j in tasks) <= 1, name=f"worker_{i}_at_most_one")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

# Data: hours required by each worker for each task
# Workers: 1=I, 2=II, 3=III, 4=IV, 5=V
# Tasks: A, B, C, D
costs = {
    (1, 'A'): 9,  (1, 'B'): 4,  (1, 'C'): 3,  (1, 'D'): 7,
    (2, 'A'): 4,  (2, 'B'): 6,  (2, 'C'): 5,  (2, 'D'): 6,
    (3, 'A'): 5,  (3, 'B'): 4,  (3, 'C'): 7,  (3, 'D'): 5,
    (4, 'A'): 7,  (4, 'B'): 5,  (4, 'C'): 2,  (4, 'D'): 3,
    (5, 'A'): 10, (5, 'B'): 6,  (5, 'C'): 7,  (5, 'D'): 4,
}

workers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
tasks = ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables: binary x_{i,j}
x = {}
for i in workers:
    for j in tasks:
        x[(i, j)] = m.addVar(vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1, name=f"x_{i}_{j}")

# Objective: minimize total working hours
obj = quicksum(costs[(i, j)] * x[(i, j)] for i in workers for j in tasks)
m.setObjective(obj, "minimize")

# Constraints: each task assigned to exactly one worker
for j in tasks:
    m.addCons(quicksum(x[(i, j)] for i in workers) == 1, name=f"task_{j}_assigned")

# Constraints: each worker assigned to at most one task
for i in workers:
    m.addCons(quicksum(x[(i, j)] for j in tasks) <= 1, name=f"worker_{i}_at_most_one")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")

import json

# Data: hours required by each worker for each task
# Workers: 1=I, 2=II, 3=III, 4=IV, 5=V
# Tasks: A, B, C, D
costs = {
    (1, 'A'): 9,  (1, 'B'): 4,  (1, 'C'): 3,  (1, 'D'): 7,
    (2, 'A'): 4,  (2, 'B'): 6,  (2, 'C'): 5,  (2, 'D'): 6,
    (3, 'A'): 5,  (3, 'B'): 4,  (3, 'C'): 7,  (3, 'D'): 5,
    (4, 'A'): 7,  (4, 'B'): 5,  (4, 'C'): 2,  (4, 'D'): 3,
    (5, 'A'): 10, (5, 'B'): 6,  (5, 'C'): 7,  (5, 'D'): 4,
}

workers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
tasks = ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables: binary x_{i,j}
x = {}
for i in workers:
    for j in tasks:
        x[(i, j)] = m.addVar(vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1, name=f"x_{i}_{j}")

# Objective: minimize total working hours
obj = quicksum(costs[(i, j)] * x[(i, j)] for i in workers for j in tasks)
m.setObjective(obj, "minimize")

# Constraints: each task assigned to exactly one worker
for j in tasks:
    m.addCons(quicksum(x[(i, j)] for i in workers) == 1, name=f"task_{j}_assigned")

# Constraints: each worker assigned to at most one task
for i in workers:
    m.addCons(quicksum(x[(i, j)] for j in tasks) <= 1, name=f"worker_{i}_at_most_one")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

# Data literals
profit_truck = 5
profit_airplane = 10
profit_boat = 8
profit_train = 7

wood_available = 890
wood_per_truck = 12
wood_per_airplane = 20
wood_per_boat = 15
wood_per_train = 10

steel_available = 500
steel_per_truck = 6
steel_per_airplane = 3
steel_per_boat = 5
steel_per_train = 4

M_truck = 74
M_airplane = 44
M_boat = 59
M_train = 89

# Create model
m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables
x_truck = m.addVar("x_truck", vtype="I", lb=0, ub=M_truck)
x_airplane = m.addVar("x_airplane", vtype="I", lb=0, ub=M_airplane)
x_boat = m.addVar("x_boat", vtype="I", lb=0, ub=M_boat)
x_train = m.addVar("x_train", vtype="I", lb=0, ub=M_train)

y_truck = m.addVar("y_truck", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_airplane = m.addVar("y_airplane", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_boat = m.addVar("y_boat", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_train = m.addVar("y_train", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)

# Objective: maximize profit
obj = quicksum([
    profit_truck * x_truck,
    profit_airplane * x_airplane,
    profit_boat * x_boat,
    profit_train * x_train
])
m.setObjective(obj, "maximize")

# Wood constraint
m.addCons(
    wood_per_truck * x_truck + wood_per_airplane * x_airplane
    + wood_per_boat * x_boat + wood_per_train * x_train <= wood_available,
    "wood_limit"
)

# Steel constraint
m.addCons(
    steel_per_truck * x_truck + steel_per_airplane * x_airplane
    + steel_per_boat * x_boat + steel_per_train * x_train <= steel_available,
    "steel_limit"
)

# Trucks exclusive of trains
m.addCons(y_truck + y_train <= 1, "trucks_exclusive_of_trains")

# Boats imply airplanes
m.addCons(y_boat <= y_airplane, "boats_imply_airplanes")

# Boats at most trains
m.addCons(x_boat <= x_train, "boats_at_most_trains")

# Upper linking constraints
m.addCons(x_truck <= M_truck * y_truck, "upper_link_truck")
m.addCons(x_airplane <= M_airplane * y_airplane, "upper_link_airplane")
m.addCons(x_boat <= M_boat * y_boat, "upper_link_boat")
m.addCons(x_train <= M_train * y_train, "upper_link_train")

# Lower linking constraints
m.addCons(x_truck >= 1 * y_truck, "lower_link_truck")
m.addCons(x_airplane >= 1 * y_airplane, "lower_link_airplane")
m.addCons(x_boat >= 1 * y_boat, "lower_link_boat")
m.addCons(x_train >= 1 * y_train, "lower_link_train")

# Solve
m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")
    print(f"x_truck: {m.getVal(x_truck)}")
    print(f"x_airplane: {m.getVal(x_airplane)}")
    print(f"x_boat: {m.getVal(x_boat)}")
    print(f"x_train: {m.getVal(x_train)}")

weak_points: Missing lower-bound linking constraint x_A >= y_A (and similarly for other binaries). Without it, y_A = 1 does not force x_A >= 1, so the formulation permits x_B > 0 while x_A = 0, violating the 'boats imply airplanes' requirement. The implication y_B <= y_A alone is insufficient without a complementary lower-bound link.

The M parameters (M_truck=74, M_airplane=44, M_boat=59, M_train=89) are sourced solely to wood availability, but their values are actually the tighter of the wood and steel upper bounds. The source attribution is misleading even though the numeric values happen to be correct.

Variable x_R is used for trains, but the letter R does not intuitively map to 'train' (unlike T, A, B for truck, airplane, boat). This reduces readability and increases the risk of transcription errors in later stages.

The binary variables y_i are not fully defined as indicators of 'x_i > 0' because only the upper-bound link (x_i <= M_i * y_i) is present. A complete indicator definition requires both x_i <= M_i * y_i and x_i >= 1 * y_i. This gap is benign for the mutual-exclusion constraint but material for the implication constraint.

import json

# Data literals
profit = {"T": 5, "A": 10, "B": 8, "R": 7}
wood = {"T": 12, "A": 20, "B": 15, "R": 10}
steel = {"T": 6, "A": 3, "B": 5, "R": 4}
wood_available = 890
steel_available = 500
M = {"T": 74, "A": 44, "B": 59, "R": 89}

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables
x_T = m.addVar("x_T", vtype="I", lb=0, ub=74)
x_A = m.addVar("x_A", vtype="I", lb=0, ub=44)
x_B = m.addVar("x_B", vtype="I", lb=0, ub=59)
x_R = m.addVar("x_R", vtype="I", lb=0, ub=89)

y_T = m.addVar("y_T", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_A = m.addVar("y_A", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)

y_R = m.addVar("y_R", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)

m.addCons(x_A <= 44 * y_A, "link_airplane")

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

# Data literals
profit_truck = 5
profit_airplane = 10
profit_boat = 8
profit_train = 7

wood_available = 890
wood_per_truck = 12
wood_per_airplane = 20
wood_per_boat = 15
wood_per_train = 10

steel_available = 500
steel_per_truck = 6
steel_per_airplane = 3
steel_per_boat = 5
steel_per_train = 4

M_truck = 74
M_airplane = 44
M_boat = 59
M_train = 89

# Create model
m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables
x_truck = m.addVar("x_truck", vtype="I", lb=0, ub=M_truck)
x_airplane = m.addVar("x_airplane", vtype="I", lb=0, ub=M_airplane)
x_boat = m.addVar("x_boat", vtype="I", lb=0, ub=M_boat)
x_train = m.addVar("x_train", vtype="I", lb=0, ub=M_train)

y_truck = m.addVar("y_truck", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_airplane = m.addVar("y_airplane", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_boat = m.addVar("y_boat", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_train = m.addVar("y_train", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)

# Objective: maximize profit
obj = quicksum([
    profit_truck * x_truck,
    profit_airplane * x_airplane,
    profit_boat * x_boat,
    profit_train * x_train
])
m.setObjective(obj, "maximize")

# Wood constraint
m.addCons(
    wood_per_truck * x_truck + wood_per_airplane * x_airplane
    + wood_per_boat * x_boat + wood_per_train * x_train <= wood_available,
    "wood_limit"
)

# Steel constraint
m.addCons(
    steel_per_truck * x_truck + steel_per_airplane * x_airplane
    + steel_per_boat * x_boat + steel_per_train * x_train <= steel_available,
    "steel_limit"
)

# Trucks exclusive of trains
m.addCons(y_truck + y_train <= 1, "trucks_exclusive_of_trains")

# Boats imply airplanes
m.addCons(y_boat <= y_airplane, "boats_imply_airplanes")

# Boats at most trains
m.addCons(x_boat <= x_train, "boats_at_most_trains")

# Upper linking constraints
m.addCons(x_truck <= M_truck * y_truck, "upper_link_truck")
m.addCons(x_airplane <= M_airplane * y_airplane, "upper_link_airplane")
m.addCons(x_boat <= M_boat * y_boat, "upper_link_boat")
m.addCons(x_train <= M_train * y_train, "upper_link_train")

# Lower linking constraints
m.addCons(x_truck >= 1 * y_truck, "lower_link_truck")
m.addCons(x_airplane >= 1 * y_airplane, "lower_link_airplane")
m.addCons(x_boat >= 1 * y_boat, "lower_link_boat")
m.addCons(x_train >= 1 * y_train, "lower_link_train")

# Solve
m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")
    print(f"x_truck: {m.getVal(x_truck)}")
    print(f"x_airplane: {m.getVal(x_airplane)}")
    print(f"x_boat: {m.getVal(x_boat)}")
    print(f"x_train: {m.getVal(x_train)}")

weak_points: Missing lower-bound linking constraint x_A >= y_A (and similarly for other binaries). Without it, y_A = 1 does not force x_A >= 1, so the formulation permits x_B > 0 while x_A = 0, violating the 'boats imply airplanes' requirement. The implication y_B <= y_A alone is insufficient without a complementary lower-bound link.

The M parameters (M_truck=74, M_airplane=44, M_boat=59, M_train=89) are sourced solely to wood availability, but their values are actually the tighter of the wood and steel upper bounds. The source attribution is misleading even though the numeric values happen to be correct.

Variable x_R is used for trains, but the letter R does not intuitively map to 'train' (unlike T, A, B for truck, airplane, boat). This reduces readability and increases the risk of transcription errors in later stages.

The binary variables y_i are not fully defined as indicators of 'x_i > 0' because only the upper-bound link (x_i <= M_i * y_i) is present. A complete indicator definition requires both x_i <= M_i * y_i and x_i >= 1 * y_i. This gap is benign for the mutual-exclusion constraint but material for the implication constraint.

weak_points: Missing lower-bound linking constraint x_A >= y_A (and similarly for other binaries). Without it, y_A = 1 does not force x_A >= 1, so the formulation permits x_B > 0 while x_A = 0, violating the 'boats imply airplanes' requirement. The implication y_B <= y_A alone is insufficient without a complementary lower-bound link.

The M parameters (M_truck=74, M_airplane=44, M_boat=59, M_train=89) are sourced solely to wood availability, but their values are actually the tighter of the wood and steel upper bounds. The source attribution is misleading even though the numeric values happen to be correct.

Variable x_R is used for trains, but the letter R does not intuitively map to 'train' (unlike T, A, B for truck, airplane, boat). This reduces readability and increases the risk of transcription errors in later stages.

The binary variables y_i are not fully defined as indicators of 'x_i > 0' because only the upper-bound link (x_i <= M_i * y_i) is present. A complete indicator definition requires both x_i <= M_i * y_i and x_i >= 1 * y_i. This gap is benign for the mutual-exclusion constraint but material for the implication constraint.

When business variables exist under different solver names, bind names instead of rewriting the model. Preserve the objective and constraints. [indicator_bidirectional_v1]
A binary indicator must be consistent with positive quantity in both directions: indicator <= quantity and quantity <= independent_upper_bound * indicator. Do not invent the upper bound. Positive evidence: IDs 9, 19, 20 and 21 recovered after scoped repair. Counterexample: indicator repair alone cannot fix a wrong business objective.
Source: work/industryor_semantic_dag_dev_v0.2

[objective_consistency_v1]

wood_per_train = 10

steel_available = 500
steel_per_truck = 6
steel_per_airplane = 3
steel_per_boat = 5
steel_per_train = 4

M_truck = 74
M_airplane = 44
M_boat = 59
M_train = 89

# Create model
m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables
x_truck = m.addVar("x_truck", vtype="I", lb=0, ub=M_truck)
x_airplane = m.addVar("x_airplane", vtype="I", lb=0, ub=M_airplane)
x_boat = m.addVar("x_boat", vtype="I", lb=0, ub=M_boat)
x_train = m.addVar("x_train", vtype="I", lb=0, ub=M_train)

y_truck = m.addVar("y_truck", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_airplane = m.addVar("y_airplane", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_boat = m.addVar("y_boat", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_train = m.addVar("y_train", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)

# Objective: maximize profit
obj = quicksum([
    profit_truck * x_truck,
    profit_airplane * x_airplane,
    profit_boat * x_boat,
    profit_train * x_train
])

    wood_per_truck * x_truck + wood_per_airplane * x_airplane
    + wood_per_boat * x_boat + wood_per_train * x_train <= wood_available,

)

This causes the cover_F constraint to be x_F + x_J >= 1 rather than the correct x_F + x_J + x_K >= 1, making the constraint overly restrictive and potentially yielding a suboptimal (larger) number of stores.

The formulation uses 12 individually named binary variables (x_A, x_B, …, x_L) rather than a single indexed variable x_i for i ∈ I. While functionally equivalent, this is less compact, harder to extend, and obscures the set-covering structure that the indexed notation makes explicit.

Because the cover_F constraint omits x_K, the model does not allow a store at area K to satisfy the coverage requirement for area F, even though the table confirms F is within 800 m of K. from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

areas = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G", "H", "I", "J", "K", "L"]

coverage = {
    "A": ["A", "C", "G", "H", "I"],
    "B": ["B", "H", "I"],
    "C": ["A", "C", "G", "H", "I"],
    "D": ["D", "J"],
    "E": ["A", "E", "G"],
    "F": ["F", "J", "K"],
    "G": ["A", "C", "E", "G"],
    "H": ["A", "B", "C", "H", "I"],
    "I": ["A", "B", "C", "H", "I"],
    "J": ["D", "F", "J", "K", "L"],
    "K": ["F", "J", "K", "L"],
    "L": ["J", "K", "L"],
}

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

x = {}
for a in areas:
    x[a] = m.addVar(vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1, name=f"x_{a}")

obj = quicksum(x[a] for a in areas)
m.setObjective(obj, "minimize")

for r in areas:
    m.addCons(quicksum(x[a] for a in coverage[r]) >= 1, name=f"cover_{r}")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")
    for a in areas:
        if m.getVal(x[a]) > 0.5:
            print(f"  Store at area {a}")

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

areas = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G", "H", "I", "J", "K", "L"]

coverage = {
    "A": ["A", "C", "G", "H", "I"],
    "B": ["B", "H", "I"],
    "C": ["A", "C", "G", "H", "I"],
    "D": ["D", "J"],
    "E": ["A", "E", "G"],
    "F": ["F", "J", "K"],
    "G": ["A", "C", "E", "G"],
    "H": ["A", "B", "C", "H", "I"],
    "I": ["A", "B", "C", "H", "I"],
    "J": ["D", "F", "J", "K", "L"],
    "K": ["F", "J", "K", "L"],
    "L": ["J", "K", "L"],
}

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

x = {}
for a in areas:
    x[a] = m.addVar(vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1, name=f"x_{a}")

obj = quicksum(x[a] for a in areas)
m.setObjective(obj, "minimize")

for r in areas:
    m.addCons(quicksum(x[a] for a in coverage[r]) >= 1, name=f"cover_{r}")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")
    for a in areas:
        if m.getVal(x[a]) > 0.5:
            print(f"  Store at area {a}")

The formulation uses 12 individually named binary variables (x_A, x_B, …, x_L) rather than a single indexed variable x_i for i ∈ I. While functionally equivalent, this is less compact, harder to extend, and obscures the set-covering structure that the indexed notation makes explicit.

Because the cover_F constraint omits x_K, the model does not allow a store at area K to satisfy the coverage requirement for area F, even though the table confirms F is within 800 m of K. from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

areas = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G", "H", "I", "J", "K", "L"]

coverage = {
    "A": ["A", "C", "G", "H", "I"],
    "B": ["B", "H", "I"],
    "C": ["A", "C", "G", "H", "I"],
    "D": ["D", "J"],
    "E": ["A", "E", "G"],
    "F": ["F", "J", "K"],
    "G": ["A", "C", "E", "G"],
    "H": ["A", "B", "C", "H", "I"],
    "I": ["A", "B", "C", "H", "I"],
    "J": ["D", "F", "J", "K", "L"],
    "K": ["F", "J", "K", "L"],
    "L": ["J", "K", "L"],
}

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

x = {}
for a in areas:
    x[a] = m.addVar(vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1, name=f"x_{a}")

obj = quicksum(x[a] for a in areas)
m.setObjective(obj, "minimize")

for r in areas:
    m.addCons(quicksum(x[a] for a in coverage[r]) >= 1, name=f"cover_{r}")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")
    for a in areas:
        if m.getVal(x[a]) > 0.5:
            print(f"  Store at area {a}")

The formulation does not explicitly state that the set of candidate store locations is identical to the set of residential areas to be covered; this assumption is only implicit in the variable definitions.

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

# Data
mfg_hours_A = 20
mfg_hours_B = 0
asm_hours_A = 5
asm_hours_B = 7
insp_hours_A = 3
insp_hours_B = 6
price_A = 650
price_B = 725
mfg_capacity = 120
asm_capacity = 80
insp_capacity = 40
mfg_cost = 12
asm_cost = 8
insp_cost = 10
min_profit = 3000
min_typeA = 5

# Profit per unit
profit_A = price_A - mfg_hours_A * mfg_cost - asm_hours_A * asm_cost - insp_hours_A * insp_cost
profit_B = price_B - mfg_hours_B * mfg_cost - asm_hours_B * asm_cost - insp_hours_B * insp_cost

# Model
m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables
x1 = m.addVar("x1", vtype="C", lb=0, ub=1000)
x2 = m.addVar("x2", vtype="C", lb=0, ub=1000)

# Objective: maximize weekly profit
m.setObjective(profit_A * x1 + profit_B * x2, "maximize")

# Manufacturing capacity
m.addCons(mfg_hours_A * x1 + mfg_hours_B * x2 <= mfg_capacity, "manufacturing_capacity")

# Assembly capacity
m.addCons(asm_hours_A * x1 + asm_hours_B * x2 <= asm_capacity, "assembly_capacity")

# Inspection capacity
m.addCons(insp_hours_A * x1 + insp_hours_B * x2 <= insp_capacity, "inspection_capacity")

# Minimum profit constraint (p1)
m.addCons(profit_A * x1 + profit_B * x2 >= min_profit, "min_profit_p1")

# Minimum Type A production (p2)
m.addCons(x1 >= min_typeA, "min_typeA_p2")

# Solve
m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")
    print(f"x1 (Type A): {m.getVal(x1)}")
    print(f"x2 (Type B): {m.getVal(x2)}")

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

# Data literals
d = [500, 550, 700, 900, 400, 300]
c = [5, 8, 10, 12, 16, 18]
F = 1200
M = [500, 1050, 1750, 2650, 3050, 3350]
n = 6

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables
x = [m.addVar(name=f"x{i+1}", lb=0, ub=M[i], vtype="C") for i in range(n)]
y = [m.addVar(name=f"y{i+1}", lb=0, ub=1, vtype="B") for i in range(n)]

# Objective: minimize variable production cost + fixed setup cost
obj = quicksum(c[i] * x[i] for i in range(n)) + F * quicksum(y[i] for i in range(n))
m.setObjective(obj, "minimize")

# Demand satisfaction (cumulative constraints)
# For each i, sum of x[j] for j >= i must be >= sum of d[j] for j >= i
for i in range(n):
    rhs = sum(d[j] for j in range(i, n))
    lhs = quicksum(x[j] for j in range(i, n))
    m.addCons(lhs >= rhs, name=f"demand_cumulative_i{i+1}")

# Fixed charge linking: x_i <= M_i * y_i
for i in range(n):
    m.addCons(x[i] <= M[i] * y[i], name=f"linking_x{i+1}")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")
    for i in range(n):
        print(f"x{i+1} = {m.getVal(x[i])}, y{i+1} = {m.getVal(y[i])}")

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

# Data literals
d = [500, 550, 700, 900, 400, 300]
c = [5, 8, 10, 12, 16, 18]
F = 1200
M = [500, 1050, 1750, 2650, 3050, 3350]
n = 6

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables
x = [m.addVar(name=f"x{i+1}", lb=0, ub=M[i], vtype="C") for i in range(n)]
y = [m.addVar(name=f"y{i+1}", lb=0, ub=1, vtype="B") for i in range(n)]

# Objective: minimize variable production cost + fixed setup cost
obj = quicksum(c[i] * x[i] for i in range(n)) + F * quicksum(y[i] for i in range(n))
m.setObjective(obj, "minimize")

# Demand satisfaction (cumulative constraints)
# For each i, sum of x[j] for j >= i must be >= sum of d[j] for j >= i
for i in range(n):
    rhs = sum(d[j] for j in range(i, n))
    lhs = quicksum(x[j] for j in range(i, n))
    m.addCons(lhs >= rhs, name=f"demand_cumulative_i{i+1}")

# Fixed charge linking: x_i <= M_i * y_i
for i in range(n):
    m.addCons(x[i] <= M[i] * y[i], name=f"linking_x{i+1}")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")
    for i in range(n):
        print(f"x{i+1} = {m.getVal(x[i])}, y{i+1} = {m.getVal(y[i])}")

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

# Data literals
d = [500, 550, 700, 900, 400, 300]
c = [5, 8, 10, 12, 16, 18]
F = 1200
M = [500, 1050, 1750, 2650, 3050, 3350]
n = 6

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables
x = [m.addVar(name=f"x{i+1}", lb=0, ub=M[i], vtype="C") for i in range(n)]
y = [m.addVar(name=f"y{i+1}", lb=0, ub=1, vtype="B") for i in range(n)]

# Objective: minimize variable production cost + fixed setup cost
obj = quicksum(c[i] * x[i] for i in range(n)) + F * quicksum(y[i] for i in range(n))
m.setObjective(obj, "minimize")

# Demand satisfaction (cumulative constraints)
# For each i, sum of x[j] for j >= i must be >= sum of d[j] for j >= i
for i in range(n):
    rhs = sum(d[j] for j in range(i, n))
    lhs = quicksum(x[j] for j in range(i, n))
    m.addCons(lhs >= rhs, name=f"demand_cumulative_i{i+1}")

# Fixed charge linking: x_i <= M_i * y_i
for i in range(n):
    m.addCons(x[i] <= M[i] * y[i], name=f"linking_x{i+1}")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")
    for i in range(n):
        print(f"x{i+1} = {m.getVal(x[i])}, y{i+1} = {m.getVal(y[i])}")

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

# Data literals
d = [500, 550, 700, 900, 400, 300]
c = [5, 8, 10, 12, 16, 18]
F = 1200
M = [500, 1050, 1750, 2650, 3050, 3350]
n = 6

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables
x = [m.addVar(name=f"x{i+1}", lb=0, ub=M[i], vtype="C") for i in range(n)]
y = [m.addVar(name=f"y{i+1}", lb=0, ub=1, vtype="B") for i in range(n)]

# Objective: minimize variable production cost + fixed setup cost
obj = quicksum(c[i] * x[i] for i in range(n)) + F * quicksum(y[i] for i in range(n))
m.setObjective(obj, "minimize")

# Demand satisfaction (cumulative constraints)
# For each i, sum of x[j] for j >= i must be >= sum of d[j] for j >= i
for i in range(n):
    rhs = sum(d[j] for j in range(i, n))
    lhs = quicksum(x[j] for j in range(i, n))
    m.addCons(lhs >= rhs, name=f"demand_cumulative_i{i+1}")

# Fixed charge linking: x_i <= M_i * y_i
for i in range(n):
    m.addCons(x[i] <= M[i] * y[i], name=f"linking_x{i+1}")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")
    for i in range(n):
        print(f"x{i+1} = {m.getVal(x[i])}, y{i+1} = {m.getVal(y[i])}")

When business variables exist under different solver names, bind names instead of rewriting the model. Preserve the objective and constraints. A binary indicator must be consistent with positive quantity in both directions: indicator <= quantity and quantity <= independent_upper_bound * indicator. Do not invent the upper bound. [objective_consistency_v1]
Recompute the business objective from semantic variables and check its direction. Goal-programming deviations are not business profit. ID 48 had feasible variables and an independent business optimum but a mismatched reported objective, and must remain rejected. Never inject a target value.

After regeneration, stale aliases can erase the export. Remove aliases whose solver names no longer exist, prefer verified canonical names, and rebind if needed. [dynamic_collection_binding_v1]
Dictionary comprehensions and simple loops may bind semantic names to expressions such as x['A']. Use only constant, code-verified index sets when repairing them. Do not guess nested or dynamic bindings. ID 19 supports this scoped mechanism; unsupported structures remain UNKNOWN.

       + veg_protein["spinach"] * y_sp + veg_protein["bell_pepper"] * y_bp
       + veg_protein["mushrooms"] * y_m)

    cost_per_g["chicken"] * x_c + cost_per_g["salmon"] * x_s + cost_per_g["tofu"] * x_t
    + veg_cost["broccoli"] * y_b + veg_cost["carrots"] * y_cr
    + veg_cost["spinach"] * y_sp + veg_cost["bell_pepper"] * y_bp
    + veg_cost["mushrooms"] * y_m <= total_budget,

    + veg_weight * y_b + veg_weight * y_cr + veg_weight * y_sp

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum

# Data
protein_per_g = {"chicken": 23/100, "salmon": 20/100, "tofu": 8/100}
cost_per_g = {"chicken": 3.0/100, "salmon": 5.0/100, "tofu": 1.5/100}

veg_protein = {"broccoli": 2.8, "carrots": 0.9, "spinach": 2.9, "bell_pepper": 1.0, "mushrooms": 3.1}
veg_cost = {"broccoli": 1.2, "carrots": 0.8, "spinach": 1.5, "bell_pepper": 1.0, "mushrooms": 2.0}
veg_weight = 100  # grams per pack

total_budget = 20
max_total_weight = 800
min_vegetable_types = 3

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables
x_c = m.addVar("x_c", vtype="C", lb=0, ub=max_total_weight)
x_s = m.addVar("x_s", vtype="C", lb=0, ub=max_total_weight)
x_t = m.addVar("x_t", vtype="C", lb=0, ub=max_total_weight)

y_b = m.addVar("y_b", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_cr = m.addVar("y_cr", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_sp = m.addVar("y_sp", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_bp = m.addVar("y_bp", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_m = m.addVar("y_m", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)

veg_vars = [y_b, y_cr, y_sp, y_bp, y_m]

# Objective: maximize protein
obj = (protein_per_g["chicken"] * x_c + protein_per_g["salmon"] * x_s + protein_per_g["tofu"] * x_t
       + veg_protein["broccoli"] * y_b + veg_protein["carrots"] * y_cr
       + veg_protein["spinach"] * y_sp + veg_protein["bell_pepper"] * y_bp
       + veg_protein["mushrooms"] * y_m)
m.setObjective(obj, "maximize")

# Constraint 1: Budget
m.addCons(
    cost_per_g["chicken"] * x_c + cost_per_g["salmon"] * x_s + cost_per_g["tofu"] * x_t
    + veg_cost["broccoli"] * y_b + veg_cost["carrots"] * y_cr
    + veg_cost["spinach"] * y_sp + veg_cost["bell_pepper"] * y_bp
    + veg_cost["mushrooms"] * y_m <= total_budget,
    name="budget"
)

# Constraint 2: Max weight
m.addCons(
    x_c + x_s + x_t
    + veg_weight * y_b + veg_weight * y_cr + veg_weight * y_sp
    + veg_weight * y_bp + veg_weight * y_m <= max_total_weight,
    name="max_weight"
)

# Constraint 3: At least 3 vegetable types
m.addCons(quicksum(veg_vars) >= min_vegetable_types, name="min_vegetable_variety")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum

# Data
protein_per_g = {"chicken": 23/100, "salmon": 20/100, "tofu": 8/100}
cost_per_g = {"chicken": 3.0/100, "salmon": 5.0/100, "tofu": 1.5/100}

veg_protein = {"broccoli": 2.8, "carrots": 0.9, "spinach": 2.9, "bell_pepper": 1.0, "mushrooms": 3.1}
veg_cost = {"broccoli": 1.2, "carrots": 0.8, "spinach": 1.5, "bell_pepper": 1.0, "mushrooms": 2.0}
veg_weight = 100  # grams per pack

total_budget = 20
max_total_weight = 800
min_vegetable_types = 3

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables
x_c = m.addVar("x_c", vtype="C", lb=0, ub=max_total_weight)
x_s = m.addVar("x_s", vtype="C", lb=0, ub=max_total_weight)
x_t = m.addVar("x_t", vtype="C", lb=0, ub=max_total_weight)

y_b = m.addVar("y_b", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_cr = m.addVar("y_cr", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_sp = m.addVar("y_sp", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_bp = m.addVar("y_bp", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)
y_m = m.addVar("y_m", vtype="B", lb=0, ub=1)

veg_vars = [y_b, y_cr, y_sp, y_bp, y_m]

# Objective: maximize protein
obj = (protein_per_g["chicken"] * x_c + protein_per_g["salmon"] * x_s + protein_per_g["tofu"] * x_t
       + veg_protein["broccoli"] * y_b + veg_protein["carrots"] * y_cr
       + veg_protein["spinach"] * y_sp + veg_protein["bell_pepper"] * y_bp
       + veg_protein["mushrooms"] * y_m)
m.setObjective(obj, "maximize")

# Constraint 1: Budget
m.addCons(
    cost_per_g["chicken"] * x_c + cost_per_g["salmon"] * x_s + cost_per_g["tofu"] * x_t
    + veg_cost["broccoli"] * y_b + veg_cost["carrots"] * y_cr
    + veg_cost["spinach"] * y_sp + veg_cost["bell_pepper"] * y_bp
    + veg_cost["mushrooms"] * y_m <= total_budget,
    name="budget"
)

# Constraint 2: Max weight
m.addCons(
    x_c + x_s + x_t
    + veg_weight * y_b + veg_weight * y_cr + veg_weight * y_sp
    + veg_weight * y_bp + veg_weight * y_m <= max_total_weight,
    name="max_weight"
)

# Constraint 3: At least 3 vegetable types
m.addCons(quicksum(veg_vars) >= min_vegetable_types, name="min_vegetable_variety")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")

When business variables exist under different solver names, bind names instead of rewriting the model. Preserve the objective and constraints. [indicator_bidirectional_v1]
A binary indicator must be consistent with positive quantity in both directions: indicator <= quantity and quantity <= independent_upper_bound * indicator. Do not invent the upper bound. Positive evidence: IDs 9, 19, 20 and 21 recovered after scoped repair. Counterexample: indicator repair alone cannot fix a wrong business objective.
Source: work/industryor_semantic_dag_dev_v0.2

[objective_consistency_v1]
Recompute the business objective from semantic variables and check its direction. Goal-programming deviations are not business profit. ID 48 had feasible variables and an independent business optimum but a mismatched reported objective, and must remain rejected. Never inject a target value.

Dictionary comprehensions and simple loops may bind semantic names to expressions such as x['A']. Use only constant, code-verified index sets when repairing them. Do not guess nested or dynamic bindings. ID 19 supports this scoped mechanism; unsupported structures remain UNKNOWN.

Variable descriptions for the vegetable pack counts (n_b, n_cr, etc.) do not explicitly state that each unit represents one 100 g pack; this is only implied by the parameter name and the weight constraint, which could lead to unit confusion.

No constraint or note addresses the possibility that Mary might want zero of a particular protein source; while the lower bound of 0 handles this, the problem narrative ('choose a combination of protein and vegetables') could be read as requiring at least one protein, which the formulation does not enforce.

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

# Data
n = 10
r = [3, 5, 2, 4, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]  # 0-indexed: r[0]=r_1, ..., r[9]=r_10
a = 10
b = 1
c = 3
p = 3
q = 1

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables (0-indexed: x[0]=x_1, ..., x[9]=x_10; s[0]=s_1, ..., s[8]=s_9; f[0]=f_1, ..., f[8]=f_9)
x = [m.addVar(vtype="I", lb=0, name=f"x_{j+1}") for j in range(n)]
s = [m.addVar(vtype="I", lb=0, name=f"s_{j+1}") for j in range(n - 1)]  # s_1 .. s_9
f = [m.addVar(vtype="I", lb=0, name=f"f_{j+1}") for j in range(n - 1)]  # f_1 .. f_9

# Objective: minimize total cost
obj = a * quicksum(x[j] for j in range(n)) + b * quicksum(s[j] for j in range(n - 1)) + c * quicksum(f[j] for j in range(n - 1))
m.setObjective(obj, "minimize")

# Repair split constraints: at end of stage j (j=1..9), all r_j tools sent for repair
for j in range(n - 1):  # j=0..8 corresponds to stage 1..9
    m.addCons(s[j] + f[j] == r[j], name=f"repair_split_{j+1}")

# Availability constraints: at stage j, tools available = r_j
# Stage j (1-indexed): x_j + (s_{j-p} if j-p>=1) + (f_{j-q} if j-q>=1) = r_j
for j in range(n):  # j=0..9 corresponds to stage 1..10
    stage = j + 1  # 1-indexed stage number
    terms = [x[j]]
    # Slow repair returns: sent at end of stage (stage - p), available at stage
    if stage - p >= 1:
        terms.append(s[stage - p - 1])  # 0-indexed: s[stage-p-1]
    # Fast repair returns: sent at end of stage (stage - q), available at stage
    if stage - q >= 1:
        terms.append(f[stage - q - 1])  # 0-indexed: f[stage-q-1]
    m.addCons(quicksum(terms) == r[j], name=f"availability_{stage}")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")

weak_points: Availability constraints use equality (=) instead of inequality (≥). For example, 'x_3 + f_2 = 2' is infeasible if f_2 > 2 (e.g., if all 5 tools from stage 2 are fast-repaired, f_2 = 5 > r_3 = 2). The correct form is x_j + (returned tools) ≥ r_j, because tools returned from prior repairs are already committed and cannot be discarded; excess tools simply sit idle without going to repair.

Because the availability constraints are equalities, the model can become infeasible for valid repair decisions made in earlier stages, which fundamentally breaks the optimization. A later formulation must replace all ten availability equalities with ≥ inequalities.

The repair-split constraints (s_j + f_j = r_j) are correct and consistent with the problem statement, but they interact incorrectly with the equality availability constraints: the split fixes the total tools entering repair, while the availability equality forces the total tools entering the stage to match r_j exactly, creating an over-constrained system when returned tools exceed demand.

weak_points: No variable or constraint tracks unused tools that carry over between stages: if more tools are available than r_j at some stage, the surplus is not modeled as available in subsequent stages, which can force unnecessary new purchases and overestimate the true optimal cost.

Availability constraints use '>=' rather than '='; combined with the absence of carry-over tracking, the feasible region is a strict subset of the true problem's feasible region, so the formulation's optimum may be worse than the true optimum.

The repair-split equalities (s_j + f_j = r_j) implicitly assume exactly r_j tools are consumed each stage, but there is no explicit 'tools used = r_j' constraint decoupled from the repair decision; the linkage is only indirect through the availability inequality.

Bounds on all variables are uniformly set to [0, 6] (the maximum r_j); while valid, tighter stage-specific bounds (e.g., s_j + f_j = r_j already caps the sum) are not exploited, which is a minor modelling inefficiency rather than a correctness issue.

weak_points: The u_j variables (surplus/inventory) are described with the source text 'If the repaired tools cannot meet the needs, new ones must be purchased', which describes the purchase decision (x_j) rather than the actual role of u_j as the carry-over surplus of unused tools. This mislabeling could confuse a later reader or reformulation.

The flow constraints are written as equalities (e.g., x_2 + f_1 + u_1 = 5 + u_2) rather than as the more transparent inequality form (available >= r_j) with a separate surplus definition. While mathematically equivalent, the equality form obscures the logical structure of 'satisfy demand, carry the remainder forward'.

The upper bounds on u_j are set to 6 (the maximum r_j) without explicit justification. While valid for optimal solutions (no reason to hold more than max demand in surplus), the reasoning is not stated, and a tighter or data-driven bound would strengthen the formulation.

The objective expression uses hardcoded numeric coefficients (10, 1, 3) rather than referencing the parameter names (a, b, c), reducing readability and making it harder to verify correctness against the parameter list.

There is no explicit terminal condition or note that tools sent for slow repair at stages 8 and 9 (s_8, s_9) return after the planning horizon (stages 11 and 12) and thus provide no benefit, only cost. While implicitly handled by their absence from later flow constraints, an explicit acknowledgment would prevent a later formulation from accidentally adding spurious return terms.

The repair-split constraints (s_j + f_j = r_j) correctly enforce that all used tools are repaired, but the formulation does not explicitly state that no repair is required after stage n (i.e., s_10 and f_10 are intentionally absent). A later reader might wonder whether this is an omission or a deliberate modeling choice.

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

# Data
n = 10
r = [3, 5, 2, 4, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]  # 0-indexed: r[0]=r_1, ..., r[9]=r_10
a = 10
b = 1
c = 3
p = 3
q = 1

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables (0-indexed: x[0]=x_1, ..., x[9]=x_10; s[0]=s_1, ..., s[8]=s_9; f[0]=f_1, ..., f[8]=f_9)
x = [m.addVar(vtype="I", lb=0, name=f"x_{j+1}") for j in range(n)]
s = [m.addVar(vtype="I", lb=0, name=f"s_{j+1}") for j in range(n - 1)]  # s_1 .. s_9
f = [m.addVar(vtype="I", lb=0, name=f"f_{j+1}") for j in range(n - 1)]  # f_1 .. f_9

# Objective: minimize total cost
obj = a * quicksum(x[j] for j in range(n)) + b * quicksum(s[j] for j in range(n - 1)) + c * quicksum(f[j] for j in range(n - 1))
m.setObjective(obj, "minimize")

# Repair split constraints: at end of stage j (j=1..9), all r_j tools sent for repair
for j in range(n - 1):  # j=0..8 corresponds to stage 1..9
    m.addCons(s[j] + f[j] == r[j], name=f"repair_split_{j+1}")

# Availability constraints: at stage j, tools available = r_j
# Stage j (1-indexed): x_j + (s_{j-p} if j-p>=1) + (f_{j-q} if j-q>=1) = r_j
for j in range(n):  # j=0..9 corresponds to stage 1..10
    stage = j + 1  # 1-indexed stage number
    terms = [x[j]]
    # Slow repair returns: sent at end of stage (stage - p), available at stage
    if stage - p >= 1:
        terms.append(s[stage - p - 1])  # 0-indexed: s[stage-p-1]
    # Fast repair returns: sent at end of stage (stage - q), available at stage
    if stage - q >= 1:
        terms.append(f[stage - q - 1])  # 0-indexed: f[stage-q-1]
    m.addCons(quicksum(terms) == r[j], name=f"availability_{stage}")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

# Data
n = 10
r = [3, 5, 2, 4, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]  # 0-indexed: r[0]=r_1, ..., r[9]=r_10
a = 10
b = 1
c = 3
p = 3
q = 1

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables (0-indexed: x[0]=x_1, ..., x[9]=x_10; s[0]=s_1, ..., s[8]=s_9; f[0]=f_1, ..., f[8]=f_9)
x = [m.addVar(vtype="I", lb=0, name=f"x_{j+1}") for j in range(n)]
s = [m.addVar(vtype="I", lb=0, name=f"s_{j+1}") for j in range(n - 1)]  # s_1 .. s_9
f = [m.addVar(vtype="I", lb=0, name=f"f_{j+1}") for j in range(n - 1)]  # f_1 .. f_9
# Inventory variables: I[j] = idle tools in pool at end of stage j+1
I = [m.addVar(vtype="I", lb=0, name=f"I_{j+1}") for j in range(n)]

# Objective: minimize total cost
obj = a * quicksum(x[j] for j in range(n)) + b * quicksum(s[j] for j in range(n - 1)) + c * quicksum(f[j] for j in range(n - 1))
m.setObjective(obj, "minimize")

# Repair split constraints: at end of stage j (j=1..9), all r_j tools used must be sent for repair
for j in range(n - 1):  # j=0..8 corresponds to stage 1..9
    m.addCons(s[j] + f[j] == r[j], name=f"repair_split_{j+1}")

# Inventory flow constraints:
# I[j] = I[j-1] + x[j] + slow_returns + fast_returns - r[j], with I[j] >= 0
# This ensures enough tools are available at each stage (I[j] >= 0 means supply >= demand)
# Slow repair: sent at end of stage (j-p+1) in 1-indexed, i.e., s[j-p] in 0-indexed, returns at stage j+1
# Fast repair: sent at end of stage (j-q+1) in 1-indexed, i.e., f[j-q] in 0-indexed, returns at stage j+1
for j in range(n):  # j=0..9 corresponds to stage 1..10
    slow_ret = 0
    fast_ret = 0
    if j - p >= 0:
        slow_ret = s[j - p]
    if j - q >= 0:
        fast_ret = f[j - q]

    if j == 0:
        # Stage 1: no prior inventory, no returns possible
        m.addCons(I[j] == x[j] + slow_ret + fast_ret - r[j], name=f"inventory_{j+1}")
    else:
        # Stage j+1: carry over idle tools from previous stage
        m.addCons(I[j] == I[j - 1] + x[j] + slow_ret + fast_ret - r[j], name=f"inventory_{j+1}")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")
    for j in range(n):
        print(f"x_{j+1} = {m.getVal(x[j])}")
    for j in range(n - 1):
        print(f"s_{j+1} = {m.getVal(s[j])}")
    for j in range(n - 1):
        print(f"f_{j+1} = {m.getVal(f[j])}")
    for j in range(n):
        print(f"I_{j+1} = {m.getVal(I[j])}")

weak_points: Availability constraints use equality (=) instead of inequality (≥). For example, 'x_3 + f_2 = 2' is infeasible if f_2 > 2 (e.g., if all 5 tools from stage 2 are fast-repaired, f_2 = 5 > r_3 = 2). The correct form is x_j + (returned tools) ≥ r_j, because tools returned from prior repairs are already committed and cannot be discarded; excess tools simply sit idle without going to repair.

Because the availability constraints are equalities, the model can become infeasible for valid repair decisions made in earlier stages, which fundamentally breaks the optimization. A later formulation must replace all ten availability equalities with ≥ inequalities.

The repair-split constraints (s_j + f_j = r_j) are correct and consistent with the problem statement, but they interact incorrectly with the equality availability constraints: the split fixes the total tools entering repair, while the availability equality forces the total tools entering the stage to match r_j exactly, creating an over-constrained system when returned tools exceed demand.

weak_points: No variable or constraint tracks unused tools that carry over between stages: if more tools are available than r_j at some stage, the surplus is not modeled as available in subsequent stages, which can force unnecessary new purchases and overestimate the true optimal cost.

Availability constraints use '>=' rather than '='; combined with the absence of carry-over tracking, the feasible region is a strict subset of the true problem's feasible region, so the formulation's optimum may be worse than the true optimum.

The repair-split equalities (s_j + f_j = r_j) implicitly assume exactly r_j tools are consumed each stage, but there is no explicit 'tools used = r_j' constraint decoupled from the repair decision; the linkage is only indirect through the availability inequality.

Bounds on all variables are uniformly set to [0, 6] (the maximum r_j); while valid, tighter stage-specific bounds (e.g., s_j + f_j = r_j already caps the sum) are not exploited, which is a minor modelling inefficiency rather than a correctness issue.

weak_points: The u_j variables (surplus/inventory) are described with the source text 'If the repaired tools cannot meet the needs, new ones must be purchased', which describes the purchase decision (x_j) rather than the actual role of u_j as the carry-over surplus of unused tools. This mislabeling could confuse a later reader or reformulation.

The flow constraints are written as equalities (e.g., x_2 + f_1 + u_1 = 5 + u_2) rather than as the more transparent inequality form (available >= r_j) with a separate surplus definition. While mathematically equivalent, the equality form obscures the logical structure of 'satisfy demand, carry the remainder forward'.

The upper bounds on u_j are set to 6 (the maximum r_j) without explicit justification. While valid for optimal solutions (no reason to hold more than max demand in surplus), the reasoning is not stated, and a tighter or data-driven bound would strengthen the formulation.

The objective expression uses hardcoded numeric coefficients (10, 1, 3) rather than referencing the parameter names (a, b, c), reducing readability and making it harder to verify correctness against the parameter list.

There is no explicit terminal condition or note that tools sent for slow repair at stages 8 and 9 (s_8, s_9) return after the planning horizon (stages 11 and 12) and thus provide no benefit, only cost. While implicitly handled by their absence from later flow constraints, an explicit acknowledgment would prevent a later formulation from accidentally adding spurious return terms.

The repair-split constraints (s_j + f_j = r_j) correctly enforce that all used tools are repaired, but the formulation does not explicitly state that no repair is required after stage n (i.e., s_10 and f_10 are intentionally absent). A later reader might wonder whether this is an omission or a deliberate modeling choice.

from pyscipopt import Model, quicksum
import json

# Data
n = 10
r = [3, 5, 2, 4, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]  # 0-indexed: r[0]=r_1, ..., r[9]=r_10
a = 10
b = 1
c = 3
p = 3
q = 1

m = Model()
m.hideOutput()
m.setRealParam("limits/time", 570)

# Decision variables (0-indexed: x[0]=x_1, ..., x[9]=x_10; s[0]=s_1, ..., s[8]=s_9; f[0]=f_1, ..., f[8]=f_9)
x = [m.addVar(vtype="I", lb=0, name=f"x_{j+1}") for j in range(n)]
s = [m.addVar(vtype="I", lb=0, name=f"s_{j+1}") for j in range(n - 1)]  # s_1 .. s_9
f = [m.addVar(vtype="I", lb=0, name=f"f_{j+1}") for j in range(n - 1)]  # f_1 .. f_9

# Objective: minimize total cost
obj = a * quicksum(x[j] for j in range(n)) + b * quicksum(s[j] for j in range(n - 1)) + c * quicksum(f[j] for j in range(n - 1))
m.setObjective(obj, "minimize")

# Repair split constraints: at end of stage j (j=1..9), all r_j tools sent for repair
for j in range(n - 1):  # j=0..8 corresponds to stage 1..9
    m.addCons(s[j] + f[j] == r[j], name=f"repair_split_{j+1}")

# Availability constraints: at stage j, tools available = r_j
# Stage j (1-indexed): x_j + (s_{j-p} if j-p>=1) + (f_{j-q} if j-q>=1) = r_j
for j in range(n):  # j=0..9 corresponds to stage 1..10
    stage = j + 1  # 1-indexed stage number
    terms = [x[j]]
    # Slow repair returns: sent at end of stage (stage - p), available at stage
    if stage - p >= 1:
        terms.append(s[stage - p - 1])  # 0-indexed: s[stage-p-1]
    # Fast repair returns: sent at end of stage (stage - q), available at stage
    if stage - q >= 1:
        terms.append(f[stage - q - 1])  # 0-indexed: f[stage-q-1]
    m.addCons(quicksum(terms) == r[j], name=f"availability_{stage}")

m.optimize()

st = m.getStatus()
print(f"status: {st}")
if m.getNSols() > 0:
    print(f"objective: {m.getObjVal()}")
